name: Pungastafur
powers: Keeps the bearer's purse heavy and money from running short.
description: Pungastafur, the purse stave of the Huld manuscript, drawn so that money would not run short and the bearer's purse would stay heavy. It belongs to the family of luck-and-money galdrastafir and was among the most sought-after signs in the grimoire tradition, a domestic charm against poverty in a subsistence economy.
source: Huld manuscript (Lbs 4626 8vo, 1860)

name: Primstav
powers: Marks the fixed and movable church feasts and the seasonal work days of the rural year.
description: A staff calendar of wood carved with notches, crosses, and figures marking the church feasts and farm year of Norway. Each primstav was tailored to its district and showed sowing, slaughter, the start of fishing, and the move up to the seter, runic signs mingling with Christian symbols. In use from the Middle Ages into the 19th century, it remains a symbol of Norwegian folk timekeeping.
source: Norwegian calendar-staff tradition; museum collections

name: Pandora's Jar
maker: Pandora, created by Hephaestus at Zeus' command
powers: Releases sorrows, sickness, and toil on humankind; hope alone remains inside.
description: The great jar or pithos that Pandora opened, releasing sorrows and evils upon humankind and keeping hope trapped inside, in Hesiod's Works and Days; the familiar 'box' is a later Latin mistranslation of pithos. Given to Epimetheus as Zeus' gift, it explains the origin of toil, sickness, and death in Greek myth.
source: Hesiod, Works and Days

name: Trident of Poseidon
powers: Shakes the earth, splits cliffs, raises and calms storms; struck rock to produce the spring on the Acropolis.
description: The three-pronged trident of Poseidon, forged by the Cyclopes, that shakes the earth, splits cliffs, and raises or calms storms; with it he struck the rock of the Acropolis to produce a salt spring in his contest with Athena. It is the standard emblem of sea power and earthquakes in Greek myth.
source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca; Homeric Hymn to Poseidon

name: Liver of Piacenza
powers: Model of a sheep's liver used in hepatoscopy; its sixteen inscribed zones map the heavens onto the organ.
description: The life-sized bronze model of a sheep's liver, found near Piacenza in 1877 and dated to the late 2nd-early 1st century BC, its surface divided into sixteen inscribed zones naming Etruscan gods; used by haruspices to teach and perform hepatoscopy, reading the future from the liver's form. It is the key artifact of Etruscan divination.
source: Archaeological find (Gossolengo, 1877; Museo Civico di Palazzo Farnese, Piacenza)

name: Pyrgi Gold Plaques
maker: Dedicated by Thefarie Velianas of Caere
powers: Bilingual dedicatory texts linking the Etruscan goddess Uni with the Phoenician Astarte; cornerstone of Etruscan language study.
description: Three gold sheets found in 1964 at the Etruscan port of Pyrgi, inscribed about 500 BC in Etruscan and Phoenician, recording Thefarie Velianas' dedication of Temple B to Uni, identified with Astarte; the bilingual text is one of the oldest historical documents from Italy and a cornerstone for understanding the Etruscan language.
source: Archaeological find (Pyrgi, Santa Severa, 1964; Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia, Rome)

name: Prydwen
powers: Arthur's vessel for voyages to the Otherworld stronghold of Annwn.
description: Prydwen, the ship of King Arthur in Welsh tradition. In Culhwch ac Olwen Arthur sails in Prydwen, and the poem Preiddeu Annwn describes Arthur's fleet journey to the Otherworld fortress of Annwn. Welsh sources also give the name to a shield, showing the word shifted between ship and protection.
source: Culhwch ac Olwen; Preiddeu Annwn

name: The Grail of Peredur
description: The dish or salver carried in the procession at the castle of Peredur in the medieval Welsh romance that bears his name. Unlike the French Grail romances, the Welsh text describes a bleeding head on a salver and a woman carrying a dish, a version that preserves a distinct Celtic Arthurian strand. The item is legendary and unattested.
source: Peredur ab Efrawg (Welsh romance)

name: Pied Piper's Pipe
powers: Its music charmed rats, and later children, following the piper out of Hamelin.
description: The pipe of the Pied Piper of Hamelin, the instrument whose music lured the town's rats to the river Weser, and then, when the townsfolk refused payment, drew the children away into a mountainside. No actual pipe survives; it belongs to the semi-legendary 1284 Hamelin tradition and its later retellings.
source: Hamelin tradition; Grimm and Browning retellings

name: The Papyrus of Ani
aliases: Book of the Dead of Ani
maker: Scribes of Thebes for the scribe Ani
powers: Guides the deceased through the judgment of the afterlife.
description: The finest surviving Book of the Dead manuscript, commissioned for the Theban scribe Ani around 1250 BCE. Its long roll of vignettes and hieroglyphic spells was meant to guide the dead through the afterlife, most famously the weighing of the heart against the feather of Ma'at in chapter 125, with Ani and his wife shown before the gods. It is the classic witness to Egyptian funerary literature.
source: The Book of the Dead (Papyrus of Ani), British Museum EA 10470

name: The Palette of Narmer
powers: Ceremonial record of the king's victory and of the unification of the Two Lands.
description: A ceremonial siltstone palette from Hierakonpolis carved around 3100 BCE, showing King Narmer smiting an enemy and reviewing decapitated captives, long read as an early record of the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt. The falcon-god Horus perched above a bound foe and the king wielding a mace set the visual language of pharaonic royal power for three thousand years.
source: Archaeological find, Hierakonpolis main deposit

name: Phurba
powers: Pins down demons during exorcism rituals
description: The three-sided ritual dagger of Tibetan Buddhism, its pommel carved with a wrathful deity's head and its blade meant to pin down demonic forces. Used by lamas in exorcism, the phurba transfixes evil at the axis between the worlds, and inscribed iron examples survive in temple collections.
source: Tibetan tantric ritual tradition; temple collections

name: Prayer Wheel
material: Metal and wood over a paper scroll
powers: Releases mantra prayers with each turn
description: The cylindrical wheel, rolled or spun in the hand, that Tibetan Buddhist practice turns to release the mantras printed inside, each revolution sending the prayer for compassion into the world. Rows of wheels line temple and stupa walls, and the device descends from Indian and Tibetan ritual turning of sacred verses.
source: Tibetan Buddhist ritual practice

name: Pachamanca
material: Heated stones dug into the earth
powers: Feeds the community and returns its first taste to the earth.
description: The Andean feast cooked by heating stones in a pit and steaming meat, potatoes, maize and herbs above them, its name meaning 'earth pot.' The cooking is tied to the land itself, and the first portion is traditionally offered to Pachamama, the earth mother, before anyone eats. Pachamanca is still prepared across the Peruvian and Bolivian highlands for festivals, weddings and planting days.
source: Andean oral tradition and contemporary practice

name: Pishtaco Knife
era: Andean folk belief to the present
powers: Cuts fat from the living to sell it in secret.
description: The blade of the Pishtaco, the feared figure of the Andes who is said to cut the fat from sleeping travelers and sell it, a belief rooted in the very real dread of the stranger in the highlands. Whistling in the dark or a shadow at the roadside is enough to raise the fear of the fat-stealer. The belief adapts, attaching to whoever the community fears most, from priests to gringos.
source: Andean folk belief and regional studies

name: Pombero Whistle
aliases: The Whistle of the Forest Imp
material: None (a sound made by the being)
era: Guaraní folk belief to the present
powers: Whistling in the night signals the trickster is near.
description: The piercing whistle that warns that the Pombero, the small naked forest imp of the Guaraní, is abroad, whistling through the countryside at dusk to frighten or to lure. He protects the birds and the wild places, punishing those who waste, and the wise leave him honey and tobacco as a peace offering. His whistle is a sound known across the Paraguayan and Argentine countryside.
source: Guaraní oral tradition

name: Puja Thali
description: Brass tray that carries the elements of Hindu worship, such as kumkum powder, turmeric, rice, flowers, incense and a burning camphor flame, as it is waved before a deity or an honoured guest. In households the thali is circulated so onlookers can receive the darshan of the flame, and the arrangement of its offerings follows the ritual order of the puja.
source: Hindu domestic ritual practice

name: Phulkari
description: Punjabi shawl or dupatta embroidered on the reverse side with silk thread so that rough, bright flower motifs bloom on the front, worked by women for weddings and festivals. A phulkari is part of a bride's trousseau, and its stitches carry the love and skill of the women who made it over months, each pattern named for the flowers and shapes it shows.
source: Punjabi folk craft tradition

name: Pashmina Shawl
description: Fine shawl woven from the under-fleece of Himalayan pashmina goats, spun and woven by Kashmiri artisans into a fabric so soft it is said to pass through a finger ring. Pashmina weaving of the Kashmir valley is famed worldwide, and the shawl is treasured as a winter garment and a symbol of the region's long craft tradition.
source: Craft history of the Kashmir valley

name: Palau Storyboard
description: Carved wooden panel of Palau recording the myths and histories of the island in low-relief figures. The gables of the bai, the men's meeting house, bore painted frieze boards recording village legend, and from the twentieth century the stories came to be carved in low-relief wood as the celebrated storyboards.
maker: Palauan carvers of the bai tradition
source: Ethnographic records of Palauan art and architecture
